value.overview: The White-lored Gnatcatcher (Polioptila albiloris) is a small, active songbird of dry tropical habitats in Mexico and western Central America. It is associated especially with thorn scrub, tropical deciduous woodland, forest edges, and regenerating vegetation. The species usually stays below about 1,000 meters and avoids the deep interior of tall, closed forest. In Costa Rica, it reaches the northwestern Pacific region, where it is most closely associated with the seasonally dry landscapes of Guanacaste and nearby areas.
value.classification: The White-lored Gnatcatcher belongs to the gnatcatcher family Polioptilidae and the genus Polioptila. Its scientific name is Polioptila albiloris.
value.identification: This is a small, slender gnatcatcher with a long tail, narrow bill, gray upperparts, and pale underparts. The white eyebrow and lore markings contrast with darker facial areas, helping distinguish it from the White-browed Gnatcatcher where their ranges overlap. Males generally show a darker crown or cap than females. It often moves actively through shrubs and low trees, frequently flicking its tail while searching for small prey.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southwestern Mexico through Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, and Nicaragua to northwestern Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly on the northwestern Pacific slope, particularly in Guanacaste and other seasonally dry lowland areas, including suitable sites around Santa Rosa and the Gulf of Nicoya region. Its habitats include arid and semiarid scrub, thorn forest, tropical deciduous woodland, woodland edges, and secondary growth, generally at low elevations and usually below 1,000 meters.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident throughout its range. In Costa Rica, it is treated as a resident species of the northwestern Pacific lowlands rather than a regular long-distance migrant; local movements may follow seasonal changes in food and vegetation.
value.breeding: Breeding has been reported mainly during the dry-season to wet-season transition and through the wetter months, broadly March to August in parts of Central America. Both adults help build a small, deep cup nest from fine plant fibers, grass, roots, and spider silk, usually placed in dense vegetation. Clutches commonly contain about four eggs. Nest parasitism by cowbirds has been recorded in parts of the species’ range.
value.dietFeeding: The White-lored Gnatcatcher feeds mainly on small insects, caterpillars, and spiders. It usually gleans prey from leaves, twigs, and bark while moving quickly through shrubs and woodland edges. It may also make short aerial sallies to capture flying insects. Its preference for open, shrubby vegetation allows it to forage in dry forest, thorn scrub, secondary growth, and other habitats with a varied but relatively low canopy.
value.behavior: This gnatcatcher is energetic and alert, commonly traveling in pairs or small family groups. It keeps in near-constant motion while searching for prey and often flicks or fans its long tail. It uses short calls and more complex songs to maintain contact and defend a territory. The species tends to remain along edges and in open woodland rather than entering dense mature forest, and it may join mixed-species foraging groups.

conservation.populationTrend: Unknown; a reliable quantified global population trend is not available.
